About: the curve of growth: how the equivalent width W of an absorption line grows with the number of absorbing atoms N

About this simulation

On screen
Left, top: the spectrum strip, yellow light whose brightness at each wavelength is Fλ/Fc, around the sodium D2 line at 589.0 nm. Left, below on the same wavelength axis: the line profile Fλ/Fc against Δλ, in a window from ±30 pm out to ±2000 pm that widens as W grows, wide enough to hold nearly all of the line's area (read the axis), the continuum at 1 dotted, the thermal core width marked above it, and a grey rectangle from 1 down to 0 whose width is the equivalent width W, marked by a double arrow. Right: the curve of growth, log10(W/pm) against log10(N/m−2), traced only where the marker has been; earlier traces stay faint grey.
Controls
N sets the number of absorbing atoms per unit area on a logarithmic slider, 1014 to 1020 m−2, with a box for log10 N and preset buttons beneath it; ▶ Play sweeps it upwards at one factor of ten every 3 s and stops at 1020. Temperature (3000 to 12000 K) sets the thermal width of the core; damping width (0.05 to 0.3 pm) sets the full width at half maximum of the damping wings. Changing either keeps the trace so far as a grey curve and starts a new one.
Measured
W = ∫(1 − Fλ/Fc) dλ, τ0 the optical depth at the line centre and the core FWHM, all from the curve-of-growth engine for a cool, non-emitting layer (Fλ/Fc = e−τ with a Voigt profile). They appear in the Readouts panel in the sidebar.
Simplifications
The layer is cool and does not emit, so a saturated line reaches zero flux; in a real stellar atmosphere the gas emits too and the core stays a little above zero, but W grows in the same three stages. One line (Na D2, f = 0.641) at one temperature and damping width throughout the layer; the D1 line at 589.6 nm, 0.6 nm away, is left out, even when the widest windows reach past it.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Doubling the atoms

Set the temperature to 6000 K, the damping width to 0.1 pm and N to 1014 m−2, and read W. Before moving N, predict what happens to W when N is doubled to 2 × 1014 m−2. Then make the change.

2 · A saturated core

Keep the temperature at 6000 K and the damping width at 0.1 pm, and set N to 1016.5 m−2, where the centre of the line has just reached the bottom. Before moving N, predict what happens to W when N is raised tenfold, to 1017.5 m−2. Then make the change.

3 · Watching the profile grow

Keep the settings of question 2 and set N back to 1016.5 m−2. Before pressing play, predict how the profile changes as N rises from here to about 1018 m−2. Then press play and watch the profile, pausing at about 1018 m−2.

4 · Heating a saturated line

Keep the damping width at 0.1 pm, set N to 1017 m−2 and the temperature to 3000 K, and read W and the thermal width. Before changing the temperature, predict what happens to W when the temperature is raised to 12000 K, which doubles the thermal width of the core. Then make the change.

5 · Very many atoms

Set the temperature to 6000 K, the damping width to 0.1 pm and N to 1019 m−2, and read W. Before moving N, predict what happens to W when N is raised tenfold, to 1020 m−2. Then make the change.

6 · Heating a very strong line

Set N to 1020 m−2, the damping width to 0.3 pm and the temperature to 3000 K, and read W. Before changing the temperature, predict what happens to W when the temperature is raised to 12000 K. Then make the change.

7 · What this shows

The curve of growth has three parts. While the line is thin (τ0 < 1), W grows in proportion to N. Once the core saturates, W grows only very slowly and depends on the temperature through the thermal width: the flat part. At large N the damping wings take over and W grows as √N, independent of temperature. Measuring W for many lines tells an astronomer how many atoms there are and how fast they move.

Adding Atoms to an Absorption Line

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Atoms in a cool gas layer take light out of the wavelengths they can absorb. This sim sends yellow light through a layer of sodium atoms, measures how much light the sodium D2 line removes, and plots that amount against the number of atoms.

What you'll learn

  • How the equivalent width W measures the light a line removes.
  • How W depends on the number of atoms per area N, and where that dependence changes.
  • What the temperature T and the damping width Γ do to W, and when they matter.
  • How a measured W gives astronomers a count of atoms.
The set-up: light with continuum flux Fc crosses a layer of N atoms per m² and emerges with flux Fλ.

What's on screen

  • Yellow strip (top left): the spectrum around the sodium D2 line at 589.0 nm, brighter where more light gets through.
  • Cyan curve: the line profile Fλ/Fc against Δλ, with the continuum dotted at 1 and the thermal core width marked above it. The grey rectangle from 1 down to 0 has width W.
  • Right panel: the curve of growth, log₁₀(W/pm) against log₁₀(N/m⁻²), drawn only where N has been; earlier traces stay faint grey.
  • Readouts: N, the centre optical depth τ0, the equivalent width W and the thermal core FWHM.
See itLook at a line that is clearly visible (N = 1015.5 m−2). Watch for: a dark band in the yellow strip, the cyan profile dipping below the dotted continuum, and a grey rectangle whose width is W.

03

The equivalent width W is the light a line removes

A line is a dip in the spectrum. Its strength is not how dark the centre looks but how much light the dip takes out, added over all wavelengths. The notes (3.43) call that the equivalent width:

Equation (3.43). Fλ is the flux per unit wavelength and Fc the continuum flux; the sim draws Fλ/Fc.

The integral is the area between the profile and the continuum. W is the width of a rectangle that reaches from the continuum down to zero and has the same area.

A line profile and its equivalent-width rectangle: the two have equal area, so the rectangle's width is W.

A spectrograph too coarse to resolve the profile blurs it but does not change the amount of light the line removes. So W can be measured even when the profile cannot be seen.

Key idea. W is an area measured as a width: the light the line removes, in units of wavelength.
See itRead W from the rectangle at N = 1016 m−2. Watch for: the grey rectangle reaching from the dotted continuum down to 0, and its width appearing as Equivalent width W in the Readouts.
04

The curve of growth has three parts, and the first is linear

Plot log₁₀ W against log₁₀ N and you get the curve of growth (notes, Figure 36b). Its three parts have different slopes.

The sim's curve of growth at 6000 K and Γ = 0.1 pm. The boundaries are approximate and move with T and Γ.

Linear part. While the line is optically thin even at its centre (τ0 below 1), each atom absorbs independently, so W is proportional to N. At 6000 K and Γ = 0.1 pm, τ0 reaches 1 near N = 1015.6 m−2, and the proportionality fades as it does.

Starting from N = 1014 m−2, doubling N takes W from 0.195 pm to 0.386 pm, a factor of 1.98. On this part W hardly depends on T or Γ.

Key idea. When every atom absorbs on its own, the light removed is just proportional to the number of atoms.
See itDouble N from 1014 m−2. Watch for: W going from 0.195 pm to 0.386 pm when the sim steps N from 1014 to 2 × 1014 m−2.
05

On the flat part a black core cannot get darker, so W grows slowly

Once τ0 is well above 1 the centre is nearly black. At N = 1016.5 m−2 (6000 K, Γ = 0.1 pm), τ0 = 8.5 and about 0.02% of the light survives at the centre. More atoms cannot take much more light out there. They can only deepen the parts of the Gaussian core still thin, and these lie further out as N grows. The Gaussian falls so steeply that W then grows roughly as √(ln N) (notes).

Raising N tenfold, from 1016.5 to 1017.5 m−2, takes W from 13.5 pm to 20.7 pm, a factor of 1.53.

How far out the core stays thick scales with its thermal width, which goes as √T. At N = 1017 m−2 and Γ = 0.1 pm, heating from 3000 K to 12000 K doubles the core FWHM (4.819 pm to 9.638 pm) and takes W from 13.0 pm to 22.2 pm, a factor of 1.70. τ0 falls from 38 to 19, yet the centre stays black: the width moved, not the depth.

Key idea. On the flat part W is set by how far the black core reaches, so it follows the thermal width and barely follows N.
See itPress Play from N = 1016.5 m−2 (6000 K, Γ = 0.1 pm). Watch for: the bottom of the profile staying at 0 while it widens into a flat floor, and W climbing only slowly.
See itAt N = 1017 m−2 and Γ = 0.1 pm, heat from 3000 K to 12000 K. Watch for: the core FWHM doubling from 4.819 pm to 9.638 pm while W rises from 13.0 pm to 22.2 pm.
06

On the damping part W grows as √N and ignores the temperature

The line has wings that fall off far more slowly than the Gaussian core, as the inverse square of the distance from the centre. The damping width Γ sets them. At large N the wings themselves turn optically thick, further and further out, and W grows as √N (notes).

From N = 1019 to 1020 m−2 (6000 K, Γ = 0.1 pm), W rises from 64.2 pm to 199 pm, a factor of 3.09 against √10 = 3.16.

Now the wings set the width, not the thermal core, so T drops out and Γ matters: W grows as √(ΓN). At N = 1020 m−2 and Γ = 0.3 pm, heating from 3000 K to 12000 K changes W from 343.8 pm to 344.1 pm, about 0.1%. Tripling Γ from 0.1 pm to 0.3 pm multiplies W by 1.73, close to √3.

Key idea. On the damping part the wings do the absorbing, so W follows N and Γ and no longer follows T.
See itRaise N from 1019 to 1020 m−2 (6000 K, Γ = 0.1 pm). Watch for: W going from 64.2 pm to 199 pm. Read the Δλ axis: the window widens.
See itAt N = 1020 m−2 and Γ = 0.3 pm, heat from 3000 K to 12000 K. Watch for: the core FWHM doubling while W stays at about 344 pm.
07

Where it matters: counting atoms in stars

  • Abundances. Astronomers compare the W of many lines of one element with a curve of growth. That gives the number of atoms per area in the lower level of each line. The Boltzmann and Saha equations (notes, section 3.2) then give the total number of atoms of the element, and so its abundance.
  • Payne's analysis and others like it showed that hydrogen is by far the most abundant element in most stars, with helium next.
  • Random speeds. The position of the flat part gives the width of the Doppler core, and so the random speeds of the atoms.
  • Limits of the sim. Its layer is cool and does not emit. In a real stellar atmosphere the gas emits too, so the core stays a little above zero, but W grows in the same three stages.
08

Summary

In one line. The equivalent width W is the light an absorption line removes, and its growth with the number of absorbing atoms has three parts, each with its own rule.
  • W = ∫(Fc − Fλ)/Fc dλ is the width of a rectangle with the line's area; blurring does not change it.
  • Linear part (τ0 below 1): W ∝ N.
  • Flat part (black core): W grows roughly as √(ln N) and follows the thermal width, so it depends on T.
  • Damping part (thick wings): W ∝ √N, set by Γ, with no dependence on T.

Common mix-ups

  • "Ten times the atoms, ten times W." Only on the linear part. From 1016.5 to 1017.5 m−2, W rises from 13.5 pm to 20.7 pm.
  • "A black core means the line has stopped growing." The sides, where the line is still thin, keep absorbing, so W keeps rising, just far more slowly than N.
  • "The damping part grows like the flat part." From 1019 to 1020 m−2, W rises from 64 pm to 199 pm, about √10-fold, not 1.5-fold.

Things to try on your own

  • At T = 12000 K, use the τ0 readout to find the N at which τ0 passes 1.
  • At N = 1017 m−2, compare W at 3000 K and 12000 K with the thermal core FWHM.
  • At N = 1020 m−2, change Γ from 0.1 pm to 0.3 pm and compare W.
